blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 24 (Organic Nitrogen Compounds), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 What are amines? Explain how they are classified, giving one aliphatic and one aromatic example of each class, and describe quaternary ammonium salts. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia in which alkyl or aryl groups replace one, two or three hydrogen atoms of NH₃. In IUPAC they are called alkanamines. The number of H atoms replaced is the basis of classification:

• Primary amines: one alkyl or aryl group is attached to the –NH₂ group. Examples: ethanamine CH₃CH₂NH₂; phenyl amine (aniline) C₆H₅NH₂.
• Secondary amines: two alkyl or aryl groups are attached to an NH group (N carries one H). Examples: N-methylethanamine CH₃–NH–CH₂CH₃; diphenyl amine (C₆H₅)₂NH.
• Tertiary amines: three alkyl or aryl groups are attached to the same nitrogen atom. Examples: N,N-dimethylmethanamine (CH₃)₃N; triphenylamine (C₆H₅)₃N.

Quaternary ammonium salts: tetra-substituted nitrogen derivatives, e.g. tetramethylammonium chloride (CH₃)₄N⁺Cl⁻.

Note: the class of an amine is decided by the branching at the nitrogen atom, not at the carbon atom attached to it; this is not the same as for alcohols or monohaloalkanes.

book_ref.quote: The number of hydrogen atoms replaced by alky or aryl groups provides a foundation

blocks.prompt: 2 Describe the preparation of primary aliphatic amines by reduction of (i) alkanenitriles (ii) nitroalkanes (iii) alkanamides. Which method gives the best yield and why? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Reduction of alkanenitriles: propanenitrile is reduced with H₂/Ni or LiAlH₄ to propan-1-amine.
CH₃CH₂C≡N + 4[H] —(LiAlH₄)→ CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂

(ii) Reduction of nitroalkanes: nitroalkanes are reduced in the presence of LiAlH₄ to primary amines.
CH₃CH₂NO₂ + 3H₂ —(LiAlH₄)→ CH₃CH₂NH₂ + 2H₂O

(iii) Reduction of alkanamides: alkanamides are reduced by LiAlH₄ (then H₂O/H⁺) to primary amines.
CH₃CONH₂ + 4[H] —(LiAlH₄)→ CH₃CH₂NH₂ + H₂O

Best yield: the reduction of alkanamides gives primary amines in good yield, since no byproduct is formed in this reaction.

book_ref.quote: Primary amines are prepared by the reduction of alkanenitriles

blocks.prompt: 3 Explain how halogenoalkanes give amines with ammonia and with primary amines. How does the ratio of reactants control the product? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Primary amines: halogenoalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution with ammonia. Excess ethanolic ammonia under high pressure is used:
CH₃CH₂Br + NH₃ (excess) —(ethanol, high pressure)→ CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HBr

Secondary amines (alkylation of primary amines): a halogenoalkane reacts with a primary amine in ethanol under pressure:
CH₃CH₂Br + CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CH₂NHCH₃ (N-methylethanamine) + HBr

Effect of ratio: the amine formed can react further with the halogenoalkane. If NH₃ is in excess, the major product is the primary amine; excess ammonia avoids the formation of secondary amines or a mixture of products. If the halogenoalkane is in excess, a tertiary amine is the major product.

book_ref.quote: Primary amines can be prepared by the nucleophilic substitution reactions of halogenoalkanes with ammonia

blocks.prompt: 4 What is the Hofmann reaction? Give its equations for ethanamide and benzamide and state its special feature. Also give the reduction of N-methylethanamide. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Hofmann reaction: an amide is treated with bromine and sodium hydroxide to give a primary amine.
CH₃CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → CH₃NH₂ + 2NaBr + Na₂CO₃ + 2H₂O
C₆H₅CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → C₆H₅NH₂ (phenylamine) + 2NaBr + Na₂CO₃ + 2H₂O

Special feature: the reaction yields the amine with one carbon less than the starting amide (the C=O carbon leaves as Na₂CO₃). Ethanamide (2 C) gives methanamine (1 C); benzamide gives phenylamine.

Reduction of an N-substituted amide gives a secondary amine:
CH₃CONHCH₃ + 2H₂ → CH₃CH₂NHCH₃ (N-methylethanamine) + H₂O

book_ref.quote: Primary alkanamine can also be prepared by the Hofmann reaction.

blocks.prompt: 5 Three amines P, Q and R have Kb = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴, 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ and 7.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ respectively. Taking pKb = –log Kb, calculate their pKb values, arrange them in order of basic strength and compare each with ammonia (pKb 4.75). Also find Kb of an amine S whose pKb is 3.50. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find each pKb from –log Kb; the smaller the pKb (larger Kb), the stronger the base. Reverse with Kb = 10^(–pKb).

book_ref.quote: The Larger the Kb (or smaller the pKb), the stronger is the base

steps: Order of basic strength (smallest pKb first): P > Q > R
Against ammonia (4.75): P (3.36) and Q (4.70) are stronger bases; R (9.13) is much weaker, like phenylamine (9.38), whose lone pair is delocalised
blocks.final_answer: pKb: P 3.36, Q 4.70, R 9.13; order P > Q > R; P and Q stronger than ammonia, R weaker; Kb(S) = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴

blocks.prompt: 6 Explain why amines are basic. Describe (i) their reaction with water (ii) salt formation with HCl, with equations, and (iii) why phenylamine is a much weaker base than ethanamine. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Basicity of amines depends on the availability of the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom, which can accept a proton.

(i) With water: water-soluble amines, like ammonia, react partially with water forming OH⁻ ions, so their solutions are weakly alkaline.
NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ (pKb 4.75)
CH₃CH₂NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ + OH⁻ (pKb 3.29)

(ii) With HCl: the nitrogen atom donates its electron pair to form a dative bond with a proton, forming a salt.
NH₃ + HCl → NH₄⁺Cl⁻
CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺Cl⁻
(Application: citric acid of lemon juice reacts with the fishy-smelling trimethylamine.)

(iii) In ethanamine the electron-donating ethyl group increases electron density on N. In phenylamine the planar nitrogen has its lone pair in a p orbital that overlaps with the delocalised π electrons of the benzene ring (Figure 24.1), so the lone pair is less available (pKb 9.38 against 3.29).

book_ref.quote: Ammonia and ethanamine react with an acid to form salts due to their basic nature

blocks.prompt: 7 How are primary, secondary and tertiary aliphatic amines distinguished by nitrous acid? Give an equation and the observation for each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Nitrous acid (nitric(III) acid) is made from NaNO₂ + HCl → HNO₂ + NaCl and added to the amine.

Primary amine: forms a diazonium salt (diazotization), which decomposes giving nitrogen gas.
CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HNO₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂N₂⁺Cl⁻ (ethane diazonium chloride) + 2H₂O
Observation: bubbles of N₂ gas.

Secondary amine: forms an N-nitrosoamine.
CH₃CH₂NHCH₃ + HNO₂ → CH₃CH₂N(NO)CH₃ + H₂O
Observation: a yellow oily liquid.

Tertiary amine: forms a soluble nitrite salt.
CH₃CH₂N(CH₃)₂ + HNO₂ → CH₃CH₂NH(CH₃)₂⁺ NO₂⁻
Observation: no visible sign of reaction.

book_ref.quote: Primary, secondary and tertiary aliphatic amines are identified and distinguished

blocks.prompt: 8 Describe the structure of phenylamine (hybridisation and delocalisation of the nitrogen lone pair) and explain its reaction with bromine water. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Structure: the ring carbons of phenylamine are sp² hybridised. The nitrogen atom is planar, with its lone pair in a p orbital, so it is also sp². This p orbital overlaps with the delocalised π electrons of the benzene ring, so the lone pair is delocalised over the ring (Figure 24.1). Phenylamine therefore gives two types of reactions: due to the benzene ring and due to the –NH₂ group.

Reaction with bromine water: the amino group is ortho-para directing, so the electrophile attacks the o and p positions. Its electrons make the ring fairly reactive, especially at these positions, so bromination is faster than for benzene and both ortho and the para positions are occupied in a single reaction:
C₆H₅NH₂ + 3Br₂ → 2,4,6-Br₃C₆H₂NH₂ (2,4,6-tribromophenylamine, white precipitate) + 3HBr

book_ref.quote: The presence of the amino group makes benzene ring fairly reactive

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe the diazotization of phenylamine: preparation of nitrous acid, conditions and equation. Why are aryl diazonium salts more stable than alkyl ones? How is phenol obtained from the diazonium salt? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Nitrous acid is unstable, so it is prepared in situ: NaNO₂ + HCl → HNO₂ + NaCl

Diazotization: phenylamine, a primary amine, reacts with nitrous acid and HCl below 10 °C (ice) to form phenyldiazonium chloride, a diazo compound with the –N⁺≡N group:
C₆H₅NH₂ + HNO₂ + HCl → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + 2H₂O
The mixture is kept below 10 °C because diazonium salts are unstable and decompose easily, giving off N₂, even at room temperature.

Stability: alkyl diazonium salts are highly unstable under all conditions and cannot be isolated. Aryl diazonium salts are fairly stable at low temperatures because the positive charge is delocalised over the aromatic ring. They are important intermediates in synthesis.

Phenol: on heating with water the diazonium salt is hydrolysed:
C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + H₂O —(heat)→ C₆H₅OH + N₂ + HCl

book_ref.quote: Phenylamine being a primary amine reacts with nitrous acid to form phenyldiazonium salt

blocks.prompt: 10 What is a coupling reaction? Explain the coupling of benzenediazonium chloride with phenol, giving the conditions, the role of the diazonium ion and the steps of the mechanism. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Coupling reaction: the reaction of an aryl diazonium salt with a strongly activated aromatic compound, such as a phenol or an amine. The products contain the –N=N– bond and are called azo compounds.

Conditions: coupling with phenol occurs in mild alkaline solution (NaOH); with aromatic amines in mild acidic conditions.

Equation:
C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + C₆H₅OH —(NaOH)→ C₆H₅–N=N–C₆H₄–OH (p-hydroxyazobenzene, orange solid) + HCl

Mechanism:
1. The positively charged diazonium ion, C₆H₅–N⁺≡N, acts as an electrophile.
2. It attacks the activated benzene ring of phenol at the para position (to –OH), forming a positively charged intermediate with H and –N=N–C₆H₅ on the same carbon.
3. The intermediate loses a proton (–H⁺), the ring is restored and p-hydroxyazobenzene, an azo compound, is formed.

book_ref.quote: Mechanism of the coupling of the diazonium ion with phenol

blocks.prompt: 11 Compare butter yellow and methyl orange as azo dyes: how each is formed, its structure and its use. What gives azo dyes their colour? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Both are made by coupling a diazonium salt with N,N-dimethylphenylamine in mild acidic conditions (ethanoic acid):

Colour: the azo group (Ph–N=N–Ph) is the chromophore, responsible for the intense colour, ranging from yellow and orange to red, blue and green depending upon the other groups attached to the benzene rings.

book_ref.quote: Coupling reaction can be used to form different types of azo dyes

rows: Product contains the azo group N=N with an –SO₃Na group
Once used in food; now forbidden as it is carcinogenic

blocks.prompt: 12 What are alkanenitriles? Describe the acid and the alkaline hydrolysis of ethanenitrile with equations, and compare the two. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Alkanenitriles are organic compounds containing the –CN functional group, e.g. ethanenitrile CH₃–CN and propanenitrile CH₃CH₂–CN. Their most important application is hydrolysis to carboxylic acids, with dilute acid or dilute alkali.

Acid hydrolysis: heated with dilute HCl or dilute H₂SO₄, a carboxylic acid is formed:
CH₃CN(aq) + 2H₂O(l) + HCl(aq) → CH₃COOH(aq) + NH₄Cl(aq)

Alkaline hydrolysis: heated with dilute NaOH, the salt of the acid forms; acidification with dilute HCl gives the free acid:
CH₃CN(aq) + H₂O(l) + NaOH(aq) → CH₃COONa(aq) + NH₃(g)
CH₃COONa(aq) + HCl(aq) → CH₃COOH(aq) + NaCl(aq)

book_ref.quote: However, the most important applications of alkanenitriles is their hydrolysis

rows: Sodium salt formed; acidify to get the acid
Nitrogen is given off as NH₃ gas

blocks.prompt: 13 Describe the preparation of amides from acyl chlorides with (i) ammonia (ii) primary amines. Why is an excess of ammonia or amine used? Explain the physical state and boiling points of amides. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Amides contain the –CO–NH₂ group; as they are prepared from carboxylic acids they are sometimes called acid amides.

(i) Acyl chlorides with ammonia:
CH₃COCl + NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ (ethanamide) + HCl
C₆H₅COCl + NH₃ → C₆H₅CONH₂ (benzamide) + HCl

(ii) Acyl chlorides with primary amines (N-substituted amides):
CH₃COCl + CH₃CH₂NH₂ → CH₃CONHCH₂CH₃ (N-ethylethanamide) + HCl
CH₃COCl + C₆H₅NH₂ → CH₃CONHC₆H₅ (N-phenylethanamide) + HCl

The reactions take place at room temperature, releasing white fumes of HCl. The HCl reacts with another molecule of ammonia or amine to form a salt (NH₃ + HCl → NH₄⁺Cl⁻; RNH₂ + HCl → RNH₃⁺Cl⁻), so an excess is used to ensure complete reaction.

Physical properties: all amides except methanamide (a liquid) are solids with sharp melting points. Their boiling points are quite high due to strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding. In N-substituted amides the melting and boiling points decrease, as the sites for hydrogen bonding diminish with more alkyl substituents.

book_ref.quote: In the above two methods, all the reactions take place at room temperature

blocks.prompt: 14 Explain, using resonance, (i) why amides are less basic than aliphatic amines and form neutral solutions, (ii) why the C–N bond of an amide is shorter than that of an amine, and (iii) why amides are the least reactive acid derivatives. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Resonance in an amide: the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised with the oxygen of the carbonyl group:
R–C(=O)–NH₂ ↔ R–C(–O⁻)=NH₂⁺

(i) Basicity: delocalisation reduces the availability of electrons on nitrogen, so amides are less basic than aliphatic amines. Unlike amines, amides form neutral solutions in water.

(ii) Bond length: resonance introduces double bond character between carbon and nitrogen, so the C–N bond in an amide (132 pm) is shorter than the usual C–N single bond in an amine (147 pm).

(iii) Reactivity: because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised over the carbonyl oxygen, the electrophilic power (+δ charge) of the carbonyl carbon decreases. Amides are therefore the least reactive of all acid derivatives; their reactions are slow and need prolonged heating or acid/base catalysts.

book_ref.quote: They exhibit resonance where the lone pair on nitrogen participates in delocalization

blocks.prompt: 15 Describe the hydrolysis (acid and base catalysed) and the reduction of amides, with equations using ethanamide and benzamide. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Reactions of amides are slow and need prolonged heating or a catalyst (acid or base).

1. Acid hydrolysis: unsubstituted amides yield the carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt.
CH₃CONH₂ + H₂O + HCl → CH₃COOH + NH₄Cl

2. Base hydrolysis: the products are the salt of the carboxylic acid and ammonia; the free acid is obtained with dilute HCl.
CH₃CONH₂ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + NH₃
CH₃COONa + HCl → CH₃COOH + NaCl

3. Reduction: amides are reduced to primary amines with lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III), LiAlH₄, in dry ethoxyethane (ether). Only the C=O is reduced; a benzene ring is unchanged.
CH₃CONH₂ + 4[H] → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + H₂O
C₆H₅CONH₂ + 4[H] → C₆H₅CH₂NH₂ + H₂O

blocks.prompt: 16 What are α-amino acids? Give their general structure, explain the formation of the dipolar ion, and describe glycine and alanine. Which amino acids are chiral, and what are essential amino acids? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Amino acids contain a basic amino group (–NH₂) and an acidic carboxylic acid group (–COOH), so they are amphoteric. The general structure (2-aminocarboxylic acid, α-amino acid) is H₂N–CH(R)–COOH; R is the part that varies.

Zwitter ion: the proton goes from the carboxyl group to the amino group within the same molecule, giving a dipolar ion with a positive and a negative end: H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻. The dipolar structure is also called the internal salt.

Glycine (aminoethanoic acid), the simplest amino acid: R = H, H₂N–CH₂–COOH.
Alanine (2-aminopropanoic acid): R = –CH₃, H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COOH.

Chirality: except glycine, all α-amino acids are chiral.
Essential amino acids are those the body cannot synthesise (they must come from food); non-essential ones the body can synthesise.

book_ref.quote: An α-amino acid exists as a dipolar ion called Zwitter ion

blocks.prompt: 17 Explain the acidic and basic properties of amino acids. Which part of the zwitter ion is acidic and which is basic? Describe the forms present at different pH and define the isoelectric point. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Amino acids are amphoteric, but they are less acidic than most carboxylic acids and less basic than most amines.

In the zwitter ion the acidic part is –NH₃⁺ (not –COO⁻) and the basic part is –COO⁻ (not –NH₂):
H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ H₂N–CH(R)–COO⁻ + H₃O⁺ (pKa ≈ 10)
H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COOH + OH⁻ (pKb ≈ 12)
RNH₃⁺ is a weaker acid than RCOOH.

Forms in aqueous solution (in equilibrium):
H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COOH (cationic, low pH) ⇌ H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻ (dipolar ion, isoelectric pH) ⇌ H₂N–CH(R)–COO⁻ (anionic, high pH)
Adding OH⁻ moves to the right; adding H⁺ moves to the left.

Isoelectric point (pI): the specific pH at which the concentration of the zwitter ion is maximum, i.e. there is no overall charge on the amino acid. Each amino acid has its own unique pI.

book_ref.quote: RNH₃⁺ is a weaker acid than RCOOH, as shown below:

blocks.prompt: 18 A mixture of four amino acids W (pI 9.7), X (pI 7.5), Y (pI 6.0) and Z (pI 3.1) is separated by electrophoresis in a buffer of pH 6.0. Predict the charge and direction of movement of each, arrange the moving ones in order of speed, and state how the spots are located. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Compare each pI with the pH: pI > pH means positive (to cathode), pI < pH means negative (to anode), pI = pH means no overall charge. The larger |pI – pH|, the faster it moves.

book_ref.quote: When an electric field is applied, the amino acids separate based on their different pI values

steps: W: pI 9.7 > pH 6.0, positive, moves to the cathode; difference = 9.7 – 6.0 = 3.7
X: pI 7.5 > pH 6.0, positive, moves to the cathode; difference = 7.5 – 6.0 = 1.5
Y: pI 6.0 = pH 6.0, no overall charge (zwitter ion), stays at the starting point
Z: pI 3.1 < pH 6.0, negative, moves to the anode; difference = 6.0 – 3.1 = 2.9
Order of speed (larger difference, faster): W (3.7) > Z (2.9) > X (1.5)
The spots are colourless; they are located by spraying ninhydrin, which gives a purple product with amino acids
blocks.final_answer: W and X to the cathode, Z to the anode, Y stays; speed W > Z > X; spots located with ninhydrin (purple)

blocks.prompt: 19 Explain the formation of a dipeptide from two amino acids. What is a peptide link, and why is the reaction a condensation? Define tripeptide and polypeptide, and find how many water molecules are lost in forming a chain of six amino acids. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Amino acid molecules can react with each other: the acidic –COOH group of one molecule reacts with the basic –NH₂ group of another. The product of two amino acids is a dipeptide:
H₂N–CH(R)–COOH + H₂N–CH(R)–COOH → H₂N–CH(R)–CO–NH–CH(R)–COOH + H₂O

Peptide link: the amide bond (–CO–NH–) between two amino acid molecules is called a peptide bond or peptide link.

Condensation: a small molecule, water, is eliminated when the reactant molecules join together.

Tripeptide: a compound formed from the condensation reaction between three amino acids.
Polypeptide: a compound formed from the condensation between a large number of amino acids.

Six amino acids in a chain: each peptide link removes one H₂O; 6 amino acids need 6 – 1 = 5 links, so 5 water molecules are lost.

book_ref.quote: The acidic -COOH group in one amino acid molecule reacts with the basic-NH₂ group in another molecule
